title: Ridgley on how much he has forgotten
summary: Ridgley says he has forgotten many things and describes his bass-singing trombone style. He says musicians then knew less theory than today's.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Okay, this is real, too, now. May Bay Ridgeley, April 7, 1961.

See, this was just so many things that I did at the time, you know. Well, of course, it's gone from the night. Sure. See, but I could do plenty of things. You know, when it came in, it would be late, and I could just grab up some time and make my different part in it that I never had been making. I went and finished the night, and I thought, well, you get that at, or something like that, you know. But of course, now, I've been away from so long, and then plenty of things, I just forgot about it. I can't bring it back to memory, but I used to do plenty of things. I sometimes like to make that little double tongue in like that a little bit, but not like Jack Carey could do it like that, but I could sing for the good, you know. The bass, singing on the trombone like that. I was really good at that. And I could play my part from the music pretty good, you see, whatever happened. I had a part that late. I could always play that pretty good too. So I was pretty good on reading just that kind of a step. But anything else, I don't know nothing about it. And plenty of things that you all asked me to do it, I don't know nothing about it. Well, I don't know anything about it either. That's a lot of the music, since the different beats and everything come out like that. And the fellas just chaps them up. Everything. Now, we had plenty of eights and quarters and halves and so on like that. But now they got plenty of faster notes to show them up. And with that time that they played, you see, and beats and everything, we didn't know as much about music like fellas know now.
